notes.1a: Credit for this part was awarded for clear explanation. Most candidates commenced by giving appropriate units for power or energy. In some cases the subsequent working and cancellations to give the result were unclear. Candidates should be reminded that it is especially important for the working to be clear in this type of question as credit is not awarded for the final answer.
notes.1i: Having written down all the units for the various components, the subsequent working was not always clear. It was common to find that the conclusion reached was ‘1 = 1’ or ‘0 = 0’.
notes.1ii: In most scripts, the calculation of the intensity in W m –2 was completed successfully. Candidates found it more difficult to convert to pW m , and many stated the answer without conversion.
notes.2i: Candidates found it difficult to focus their answer on the specific situation given. In very few answers was a reference made to the signal generator being connected to both loudspeakers.
notes.2ii: In each part, it was expected that the phase angle or path difference would be quoted and then the effect on the resultant displacement stated. There were few fully correct answers. Many candidates stated general conditions for phase difference. Others made reference to path difference but then confused this with phase angle.
notes.2b: There were some very carefully drawn curves but many answers could be credited only for a correct period or a correct amplitude.
notes.3i: Generally, it was stated that the air resistance would increase as the velocity increases, giving rise to a reducing acceleration. Often there was no reference to the resultant force or there was a statement that the final acceleration would be zero.
notes.3ii: Candidates found this difficult. The most common mistake was to assume that the force due to air resistance was the accelerating force.
notes.3iii: A small number of candidates made a correct reference to the fact that, at a speed of 60 m s –1 , the air resistance is less than the weight. Most attempted an unsuccessful explanation based on the fact that the graph extends beyond 60 m s .
notes.4i: This question concerned work done, but very few answers involved energy. In many answers there was some discussion of forces in equilibrium.
notes.4ii: Candidates should be encouraged to use terms such as ‘equal and opposite’, rather than ‘cancels out’ or ‘balanced’. The use of imprecise terminology frequently meant that credit could not be
notes.5i: Again, there were very few problems with this calculation.
notes.5ii: This was completed successfully in most scripts.
notes.5iii: With few exceptions, candidates did give a correct expression for power. Many candidates found it difficult to substitute appropriate values of current and resistance into the equations. It may be helpful for candidates to write the currents on the circuit diagram to avoid confusing the currents in different branches of the circuit.
notes.6a: This was answered well in many scripts. A common problem was to omit to state that the reflected wave interferes/overlaps with the incident wave.
notes.6i: The most common answers were 0.68 m and 0.34 m. Only a small number of candidates determined correct values.
notes.6ii: On those diagrams where more than one node and one antinode were labelled, intermediate nodes and antinodes were sometimes not equally spaced. Frequently, a node or an antinode was shown at the centre of the tube.
notes.7a: In most scripts, a correct expression was quoted for stress in terms of force and area. The most common problems were associated with either taking 15 as the area in m or with powers-of-ten when converting mm to m . Candidates may benefit from further practice at unit conversions.
notes.7b: Density involves mass and there was some confusion as to the use of g. Some weaker candidates incorrectly attempted to base their answer on the expression R = ρL/A, perhaps because it involves length and area.
notes.8a: Many suggestions were made. Candidates should avoid referring to mass and energy separately in this type of question; ‘mass-energy’ is the preferred term for the conserved quantity. Candidates should be advised as to the correct use of terms such as ‘proton number’, ‘number of protons’, ‘nucleon number’ and ‘number of neutrons’.
notes.8i: This part was completed successfully by a significant number of candidates.
notes.8ii: There were few correct solutions. In general, candidates did not use the expression given in (b)(i). A common mistake was to calculate the speed of the α-particle and then to assume that this would be the speed of the thorium nucleus.
notes.key_messages: • There are a number of questions on the paper that require general recall. Candidates should review the learning objectives and ensure they are well prepared to give correct answers to this type of question. • Candidates should be reminded that, where a question asks for a statement and an explanation, the explanation is essential to receive full credit. notes.general_comments: General Comments The time constraint of one hour does make the paper a challenge: it demands quick and accurate working by candidates. The average time of 90 seconds per answer is made possible by having many questions that can be answered after a quick (but careful) read through the question. Candidates should be advised never to spend a disproportionately long time on any one question. They should also be advised to use the spaces on the question paper for their working. Care with units is essential. Prefix errors are a cause of many wrong answers as are corresponding power-of-ten errors. The candidates found Questions 1, 18 and 27 relatively easy. Questions 5, 11, 19, 33 and 35 were difficult.
